scribe_response.text: Is there a celebration you remember especially well? A celebration I uh remember especially well is my own wedding, in nineteen um eighty-one. I had come home from Abu Dhabi for one month, and the whole family had been planning for a year. The wedding took place at a temple near Guruvayur, in the cool early morning. Lakshmi wore a cream and gold sari, and she kept her eyes lowered until the very last ritual. Her father tied the uh sacred thread with hands that trembled slightly. The priest chanted in a low voice, and the smell of camphor drifted around us. I wore a white mundu and a silk shawl, and I was so nervous that my hands shook. My father arranged everything, from the priest to the flowers, with the care of a man marking an examination. The pandal was built from bamboo and coconut fronds, and it smelled wonderfully of green leaves. The cooks arrived at four in the morning to light the great wood fires. The bride's family had decorated the entrance with fresh jasmine strings. Over three hundred guests came, and the banana leaves were laid out in long rows on the floor. A photographer from Thrissur set up a tripod and made everyone stand still. What happened next? The children were given small sweets, and they hid the um wrappers in their pockets. My aunt pressed a coin into my hand for luck. The feast began with a pinch of salt and a spoonful of plain rice, and then came the endless dishes. There was sambar, avial, olan, a sweet pumpkin curry, three kinds of pickle, and crisp banana chips. The payasam arrived at the end in great brass vessels, and the cooks ladled it out with long spoons. I believe I told you about my shoes and the Madras train last time. At the temple door I had to leave my shoes outside, and my cousins, who knew the old story, laughed at me. One of them even stood guard over my footwear for the whole ceremony. Back to um the feast, my mother and her sisters had cooked for two days without sleeping. My uncle Raman insisted on carrying the pickle jar himself, because he did not trust the servers. There was a small band with a clarinet and drums, and they played film songs from the nineteen sixties. My sister Radha danced with her friends, and Meena sang uh a verse from a Carnatic composition. Her voice was clear and true, and the elders went quiet to listen. Can you tell me more about that? I was very moved, because I knew that she had practised for weeks in secret. Lakshmi and I walked around the sacred, sacred fire seven times, and each round felt like a promise. Her bangles rang softly, and I could uh hear them above the music. In the afternoon the rain came suddenly, and everyone ran under the pandal laughing. The water dripped through the fronds, and the children stamped in um the puddles. I remember thinking that um the rain had come to bless us, just as it blessed our house in my childhood. By evening the guests had left, and a tired quiet, quiet settled over the courtyard. Lakshmi and I sat on the verandah, and she asked me whether I was happy. I said uh that I was happier than I could measure, which for an um engineer is a great confession. She laughed, and I knew then that I had married someone who understood me. Our photographs from that day have faded to brown, but my memory of it is still in colour. We celebrated our fortieth anniversary with a small dinner, and my sons made a toast. They asked for the old story of the wedding feast, and I told it again. I think a good celebration is one that you can taste years afterwards.
